title: The desert mothers
hook: Syncletica and others taught that the heart must be tended like a fire

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was abba, father, the desert's name for a wise elder. Your line was give me a word.

Have you ever tried to light a fire with damp wood? A campfire, a wood stove, a fireplace in an old house. You crouch down and blow, and for a long time you get nothing but smoke. It stings your eyes. You're sure it's not going to work. Then, if you keep at it, one small flame catches, then another, and suddenly there's warmth. A woman of the Egyptian desert used that very picture for the life of prayer. Today's word is what people called her: amma.
screen: `DAMP WOOD.` → `SMOKE IN YOUR EYES.` → `ONE FLAME CATCHES.`

segments.voice: The desert mothers were there too, and people walked out to them just the same as to the abbas. The title was amma, mother, the female twin of abba. Their sayings sit in the same old collections alongside the men's, fewer of them, but sharp. One of them is Amma Syncletica of Alexandria. Tradition says she was a well-off young woman who gave away her inheritance and went to live a life of prayer outside the city, and that younger women gathered around her to learn. Her saying about fire goes like this, in paraphrase: at the beginning, anyone who draws near to God has a hard struggle, and afterward, a joy that can't be put into words. It's like people lighting a fire. First the smoke, and tears in their eyes, and then they get what they wanted. So we too have to kindle the divine fire in ourselves, with tears and effort. Notice what she doesn't say. She doesn't say the smoke means you're doing it wrong. The smoke is part of lighting fires. She also said something that fits a life of jobs and kids and phones: many who live alone in the mountains behave as if they're in town, and it's possible to live in a crowd and keep solitude in your mind. Another desert mother, Amma Sarah, is remembered for wrestling with one temptation for thirteen years. She never prayed for it to vanish. She prayed for strength. That's tending a fire: not a single blaze, but going back again and again, blowing gently on the coals.
screen: `AMMA: MOTHER.` · `SYNCLETICA OF ALEXANDRIA.` · `FIRST THE SMOKE, THEN THE FLAME.` · `SOLITUDE IN A CROWD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing that has gone cold: a habit of prayer, a friendship, a creative project, reading, running, kindness to someone difficult. Don't try to rebuild the bonfire; just picture blowing gently on the coals, one small breath. If there's smoke, that's normal.
Amma. Mother, the twin of abba. The desert's name for its wise women.
Your line: tend the fire. Smoke comes first, and then the flame. Day two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians, especially in Orthodox and Catholic monastic communities, read the sayings of the desert mothers alongside the fathers, and some women serve as spiritual mothers who guide others in prayer.

original.note: Greek form of an Aramaic word for mother; the desert's title for a wise woman.

trapdoor: what you thought: the desert saints were all men.
what it means: women were there too; they taught that the heart is a fire you keep tending, through smoke and all.
what a scholar hears: the ammas in the Apophthegmata; a fifth-century Life of Syncletica; and a saying that solitude is first a matter of the mind.
